title: Book 14 — Odysseus in the hut with Eumaeus
paragraphs: Odysseus now left the harbor and took the rough path up through the wooded country and over the mountain crest until he reached the place where Athena had told him he would find the swineherd, the most thrifty servant he had. He found him sitting in front of his hut, close to the pig yards he had built on a site that could be seen from far off. He had made them spacious and handsome, with plenty of room for the pigs to range around them. He had built them during his master’s absence, out of stones he had gathered from the ground, without telling Penelope or Laertes, and had topped them with a hedge of thorn bushes. Outside the yard he had run a strong fence of split oak posts set close together, and inside he had built twelve pens next to one another for the sows to lie in. Fifty pigs wallowed in each pen, all of them breeding sows, but the boars slept outside and were far fewer, since the suitors kept eating them and the swineherd had to keep sending them his best. There were three hundred and sixty boar pigs, and the herdsman’s four dogs, as fierce as wolves, always slept among them. The swineherd himself was at that moment cutting a pair of sandals from a good thick ox hide. Three of his men were out herding the pigs in various places, and he had sent the fourth to town with a boar he had been forced to give the suitors, so they could sacrifice it and feast on the meat.

When the dogs saw Odysseus, they set up a furious barking and rushed at him, but Odysseus was cunning enough to sit down and let go of the stick in his hand. Even so, they would have torn him apart right there in his own homestead if the swineherd hadn’t dropped his ox hide, run at full speed through the yard gate, and driven the dogs off by shouting and throwing stones at them. Then he said to Odysseus, “Old man, the dogs very nearly made short work of you, and that would have gotten me into trouble. The gods have given me enough to worry about without that—I’ve lost the best of masters, and I grieve for him constantly. I have to tend pigs for other men to eat, while he, if he’s still alive to see the light of day, is starving in some distant land. But come inside, and once you’ve had your fill of bread and wine, tell me where you’re from and all about your troubles.”

At this the swineherd led the way into the hut and told him to sit down. He spread a good thick bed of rushes on the floor, and on top of it he threw the shaggy chamois skin—a great thick one—that he used to sleep on at night. Odysseus was glad to be welcomed so warmly and said, “May Zeus, sir, and the rest of the gods grant you your heart’s desire, in return for the kindness you have shown me.”

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “Stranger, even if a poorer man than you came here, it wouldn’t be right for me to insult him, since all strangers and beggars come from Zeus. You must take what you’re given and be grateful, for servants live in fear when they have young lords for masters—and that is my misfortune now, since heaven has kept from coming home the man who would always have been good to me. He would have given me something of my own: a house, a piece of land, a good-looking wife, and everything else a generous master gives a servant who has worked hard for him—for the gods have blessed my labor in the position I hold. If my master had grown old here, he would have done great things for me, but he’s gone—and I wish Helen’s whole family were utterly destroyed, for she has been the death of many a good man. It was this business that took my master to Ilius, the land of noble horses, to fight the Trojans for King Agamemnon’s cause.”

As he spoke, he tied his belt around him and went to the pens where the young suckling pigs were kept. He picked out two, brought them back, and sacrificed them. He singed them, cut them up, and put them on spits; when the meat was cooked, he brought it all in and set it before Odysseus, hot and still on the spit, and Odysseus sprinkled it with white barley meal. The swineherd then mixed wine in a bowl of ivy wood, and taking a seat across from Odysseus, told him to begin.

“Dig in, stranger,” he said, “to a dish of servants’ pork. The fat pigs go to the suitors, who eat them up without shame or restraint, but the blessed gods take no pleasure in such shameless behavior—they honor those who act lawfully and rightly. Even fierce raiders who go plundering other men’s land, whose spoils Zeus himself grants them, come home with troubled consciences once their ships are full, and look fearfully for judgment to come. But some god seems to have told these people that Odysseus is dead and gone, so instead of going back to their own homes and making their offers of marriage in the usual way, they lay waste to his estate by force, without fear or limit. Not a day or night comes from heaven but they sacrifice not just one or two victims, and they drink freely of his wine, for he was extremely rich. No other great man, either in Ithaca or on the mainland, is as rich as he was—he had as much as twenty men put together. I’ll tell you everything he owned. There are twelve herds of cattle on the mainland and as many flocks of sheep, twelve droves of pigs besides, and his own men and hired strangers tend twelve far-ranging herds of goats for him. Here in Ithaca he keeps large flocks of goats too, out at the far end of the island, in the charge of excellent goatherds. Each of these men sends the suitors the best goat in his flock every day. As for me, I’m in charge of the pigs you see here, and I have to keep picking out the best of them and sending it to the suitors.”

This was his story, but Odysseus went on eating and drinking ravenously without a word, brooding over his revenge. When he had eaten his fill and was satisfied, the swineherd took the bowl he usually drank from, filled it with wine, and handed it to Odysseus, who was pleased and said as he took it in his hands, “My friend, who was this master of yours who bought you and paid for you, so rich and powerful as you describe him? You say he died in King Agamemnon’s cause—tell me who he was, in case I have met such a man. Zeus and the other gods know, but I may be able to give you news of him, for I have traveled widely.”

Eumaeus answered, “Old man, no traveler who comes here with news will get Odysseus’s wife and son to believe his story. Even so, tramps looking for a bed keep turning up with their mouths full of lies and not a word of truth in them. Everyone who makes his way to Ithaca goes to my mistress and tells her falsehoods, and she takes them in, makes a fuss over them, and asks them every kind of question, crying the whole time the way women do when they’ve lost their husbands. And you too, old man, would doubtless spin a pretty story for a shirt and a cloak. But the wolves and birds of prey tore Odysseus to pieces long ago, or the fish of the sea have eaten him, and his bones lie buried deep in sand on some foreign shore. He is dead and gone, and it’s a bad business for all his friends—for me most of all. Wherever I go, I will never find so good a master again, not even if I went home to my own mother and father, where I was born and raised. I don’t care so much about my parents now, though I would dearly love to see them again in my own country. It’s the loss of Odysseus that grieves me most. I can’t speak of him without reverence, even though he is no longer here, for he was very fond of me and took such care of me that wherever he is, I will always honor his memory.”

“My friend,” Odysseus replied, “you are very sure of yourself, and very reluctant to believe your master will ever come home—but I won’t just say it, I’ll swear to it: he is coming. Give me nothing for my news until he has actually returned; then you may give me a shirt and cloak of good quality if you wish. I am in great need, but I won’t take anything at all before then, for I hate a man who lets his poverty tempt him into lying as much as I hate the fires of hell. I swear by King Zeus, by the rites of hospitality, and by that hearth of Odysseus to which I have now come, that everything will happen exactly as I have said. Odysseus will return this very year; between the end of this moon and the start of the next, he will be here to take vengeance on all those who are mistreating his wife and son.”

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “Old man, you will get no reward for bringing good news, nor will Odysseus ever come home. Drink your wine in peace, and let’s talk about something else—don’t keep reminding me of all this, it always pains me when anyone speaks of my honored master. As for your oath, we’ll let it be, but I only wish he would come, as do Penelope, his old father Laertes, and his son Telemachus. I’m terribly troubled too about that boy of his. He was growing fast into manhood, and promised to be every bit the man his father was, in face and figure, but someone, god or man, has unsettled his mind, so he has gone off to Pylos to try to get news of his father—and the suitors are lying in wait for him on his way home, hoping to wipe the house of Arceisius—Odysseus’s grandfather—from memory in Ithaca. But let’s say no more about him, and leave him to be caught, or to escape, if the son of Cronus holds his hand over him to protect him. And now, old man, tell me your own story. Tell me too, since I want to know, who you are and where you come from. Tell me about your city and your parents, what kind of ship brought you, how the crew got you to Ithaca, and what country they claimed to be from—for you can’t have come here by land.”

And Odysseus answered, “I will tell you the whole story. If there were meat and wine enough, and we could stay here in the hut with nothing to do but eat and drink while the others went off to their work, I could easily talk for a full twelve months without ever finishing the tale of the sorrows heaven has seen fit to send me.

“I am a Cretan by birth. My father was a well-to-do man who had many sons born to him in marriage, but I was the son of a slave woman he had bought as a concubine. All the same, my father, Castor son of Hylax, treated me as an equal to my brothers born in wedlock. It is his lineage I claim, and he was held in the highest honor among the Cretans for his wealth, his prosperity, and the courage of his sons. But when death carried him off to the house of Hades, his sons divided his property and cast lots for their shares, and to me they gave a holding and little else. Even so, my own courage won me a rich wife, for I was never one to boast or hang back on the battlefield. It’s all over now, but if you look at the straw that’s left, you can still see what the grain was, for I have had more trouble than I can tell. Ares and Athena made me formidable in war. When I picked my men to spring an ambush on the enemy, I never gave death a single thought, but was always first to leap forward and spear any man I could overtake. That was the kind of soldier I was, but I never cared for farm work, or for the frugal life of a man raising children at home. My delight was in ships, fighting, javelins, and arrows—things most men shudder even to think of, but each man is drawn to what he’s drawn to, and this was my nature. Before the Achaeans sailed for Troy, I commanded men and ships on foreign campaigns nine times, and gathered a great deal of wealth. I took my pick of the spoils first, and still more fell to me afterward.

“My house grew quickly, and I became a great man among the Cretans, but when Zeus planned that terrible campaign in which so many died, the people required Idomeneus and me to lead their ships to Troy, and there was no way around it, for they insisted we do it. We fought there nine full years, and in the tenth we sacked the city of Priam and sailed for home as heaven scattered us. It was then that Zeus devised evil against me. I spent only one happy month with my children, my wife, and my property, and then I got the idea of raiding Egypt, so I fitted out a fine fleet and manned it. I had nine ships, and men flocked to fill them. For six days my men and I feasted, and I supplied many victims, both for sacrifice to the gods and for the men to eat, and on the seventh day we went aboard and set sail from Crete with a fair north wind behind us, sailing as smoothly as if we were going down a river. Nothing went wrong with any of our ships, and none of us fell sick, so we simply sat and let the ships go where the wind and the steersmen took them. On the fifth day we reached the river Aegyptus, and there I anchored my ships in the river, telling my men to stay by them and keep watch while I sent out scouts to look things over from every vantage point.

“But my men disobeyed my orders, went off on their own, and ravaged the land of the Egyptians, killing the men and carrying off their wives and children. The alarm quickly reached the city, and at the sound of the war cry the people came out at daybreak, until the whole plain was filled with horsemen, foot soldiers, and the gleam of armor. Then Zeus threw my men into a panic, and they could no longer stand and face the enemy, for they found themselves surrounded. The Egyptians killed many of us and took the rest alive to work as slaves for them. Zeus, though, put an idea into my mind—and I wish now I had died there in Egypt instead, for there was much grief still waiting for me—I took off my helmet and shield and let my spear drop from my hand, then went straight to the king’s chariot, clasped his knees, and kissed them. At that he spared my life, told me to climb into his chariot, and drove me home, weeping, to his own house. Many men rushed at me with their ash spears, furious, trying to kill me, but the king protected me, for he feared the anger of Zeus, protector of strangers, who punishes those who do wrong.

“I stayed there seven years and gathered a good deal of money among the Egyptians, for they all gave me something. But when it was going on for the eighth year, a certain Phoenician turned up, a cunning rogue who had already done all kinds of mischief, and he talked me into going with him to Phoenicia, where his house and property were. I stayed there a full twelve months, and at the end of that time, when the months and days had passed until the same season came round again, he put me aboard a ship bound for Libya, claiming I was to carry cargo there with him, when really he meant to sell me as a slave and pocket the money. I suspected what he was up to, but I went aboard with him anyway, for I had no choice.

“The ship ran before a fresh north wind until we reached the sea that lies between Crete and Libya. There, however, Zeus planned their destruction, for as soon as we were well clear of Crete and could see nothing but sea and sky, he raised a black cloud over our ship and the sea grew dark beneath it. Then Zeus let fly with his thunderbolts, and the ship spun round and round and was filled with fire and brimstone as the lightning struck it. The men all fell into the sea; they were carried about in the water round the ship, looking like so many seagulls, but the god soon deprived them of any chance of getting home again. I was in despair, but Zeus put the ship’s mast within my reach, which saved my life, for I clung to it and drifted before the fury of the gale. I drifted for nine days, and in the darkness of the tenth night a great wave carried me onto the Thesprotian coast. There Pheidon, king of the Thesprotians, took me in and treated me kindly without asking anything in return—his son found me nearly dead with cold and exhaustion, lifted me up by the hand, took me to his father’s house, and gave me clothes to wear.

“There it was that I heard news of Odysseus, for the king told me he had welcomed him and shown him great hospitality while he was on his way home. He also showed me the treasure of gold and worked iron that Odysseus had gathered—enough to support his family for ten generations; that was how much he had left in King Pheidon’s house. But the king said Odysseus had gone to Dodona to learn Zeus’s will from the god’s tall oak tree, to find out whether, after so long an absence, he should return to Ithaca openly or in secret. The king even swore to me, pouring drink offerings in his own house as he did it, that the ship was ready by the shore, and the crew found, to carry him to his own country. He sent me off, though, before Odysseus returned, since a Thesprotian ship happened to be sailing for the wheat-growing island of Dulichium, and he told the men in charge of her to be sure to see me safely to King Acastus.

“These men hatched a plot against me that would have brought me to the very depths of misery, for once the ship had gone some way from land, they decided to sell me as a slave. They stripped me of the shirt and cloak I was wearing and gave me instead the tattered rags you see on me now. Then, toward nightfall, they reached the cultivated land of Ithaca, and there they tied me fast in the ship with a strong rope while they went ashore to get their supper by the sea. But the gods soon loosened my bonds, and after pulling my rags over my head, I slid down the rudder into the sea, struck out, and swam until I was well clear of them, then came ashore near a thick wood, where I lay hidden. They were furious that I had escaped and searched all around for me, until at last they gave it up and went back to their ship. The gods, having hidden me so easily, then led me to a good man’s door—it seems I am not meant to die just yet.”

To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “Poor unlucky stranger, I found the story of your troubles truly interesting, but that part about Odysseus isn’t right, and you will never get me to believe it. Why does a man like you go around telling lies this way? I know all there is to know about my master’s return. The gods, every one of them, hate him, or they would have let him die at Troy, or die among his friends once his fighting was done—then the Achaeans would have built a mound over his ashes and his son would have inherited his renown. But instead the storm winds have carried him off, and we don’t know where.

“As for me, I live out here away from everything, with the pigs, and I never go into town unless Penelope sends for me when some news comes about Odysseus. Then everyone gathers around and asks questions—those who grieve over the king’s absence, and those who are glad of it because they can eat up his property without paying for it. For my own part, I’ve stopped asking anyone else since the time I was taken in by an Aetolian, a man who had killed someone and traveled far before he finally reached my post, and I treated him kindly. He said he had seen Odysseus among the Cretans with Idomeneus, refitting his ships, which had been damaged in a storm, and that Odysseus would return the following summer or autumn with his men and bring back great wealth. And now you, you unlucky old man, since fate has brought you to my door, don’t try to win me over this way with false hopes. It isn’t for any such reason that I’ll treat you kindly, but only out of respect for Zeus, god of hospitality, because I fear him and pity you.”

Odysseus answered, “I see you are not a man who believes easily. I have given you my oath, and still you won’t take my word for it. Let us make a bargain, then, and call every god in heaven to witness it. If your master comes home, give me a cloak and shirt of good quality and send me on my way to Dulichium, where I want to go. But if he doesn’t come as I say he will, set your men on me and have them throw me from that cliff over there, as a warning to tramps not to go around the country telling lies.”

“And a fine figure I’d cut then,” replied Eumaeus, “both now and afterward, if I killed you after taking you into my hut and showing you hospitality. I would need to say my prayers in dead earnest if I did that. But it’s just about supper time, and I hope my men will be in soon, so we can cook something good for supper.”

Thus they talked, and presently the other swineherds came up with the pigs, which were shut up for the night in their pens, squealing tremendously as they were driven in. Eumaeus called out to his men, “Bring in the best pig you have, so I can sacrifice him for this stranger, and we’ll take our own share of him too. We’ve had trouble enough all this time feeding pigs, while others reap the reward of our labor.”

At this he began chopping firewood, while the others brought in a fine fat five-year-old boar and set it by the altar. Eumaeus did not forget the gods, for he was a man of sound principle, so the first thing he did was cut bristles from the pig’s forehead and throw them into the fire, praying to all the gods as he did it that Odysseus might come home again. Then he clubbed the pig with a length of oak he had kept back from the firewood and stunned it, and the others slaughtered it and singed it. They cut it up, and Eumaeus began by taking raw pieces from each joint and laying them on some of the fat, sprinkling them with barley meal and setting them on the embers. The rest of the meat they cut up small, put on spits, and roasted until it was done; then they took it off the spits and piled it on the serving table. The swineherd, who was a scrupulously fair man, stood up to give everyone his share. He made seven portions—one he set aside for Hermes, son of Maia, and the nymphs, praying to them as he did so, and the rest he divided among the men one by one. He gave Odysseus slices cut lengthwise down the loin, as a mark of special honor, and Odysseus was very pleased. “I hope, Eumaeus,” he said, “that Zeus will think as well of you as I do, for the respect you’re showing to an outcast like me.”
To this you answered, swineherd Eumaeus, “Eat, my good man, and enjoy your supper, such as it is. God gives this and withholds that, just as he sees fit, for he can do whatever he pleases.”

As he spoke, he cut off the first piece and offered it as a burnt sacrifice to the immortal gods, then poured them a drink offering, put the cup into Odysseus’s hands, and sat down to his own share. Mesaulius brought them their bread—the swineherd had bought this man himself, from among the Taphians, during his master’s absence, paying for him out of his own money without telling either his mistress or Laertes. They then set to work on the good food before them, and when they had eaten and drunk their fill, Mesaulius cleared away what was left of the bread, and they all went to bed after a hearty supper.

Now the night came on stormy and very dark, for there was no moon. The rain poured without stopping, and the wind blew hard out of the west, which brings wet weather, so Odysseus thought he would test whether Eumaeus, for all his good care of him, would take off his own cloak and give it to him, or have one of his men do it. “Listen to me, Eumaeus, and the rest of you,” he said. “Once I’ve said a prayer, I’ll tell you something. It’s the wine talking—wine will set even a wise man singing, make him laugh and dance and say things better left unsaid, but since I’ve started, I’ll go on. If only I were still young and strong as when we set up an ambush outside the walls of Troy. Menelaus and Odysseus were the leaders, but I had a command too, since the other two wanted it that way. When we had come up under the city wall, we crouched down in our armor and lay hidden among the reeds and thick brush growing around the marsh. It turned to frost, with a north wind blowing—the snow fell fine and small like hoarfrost, and our shields were coated thick with ice. The others all had cloaks and shirts, and slept comfortably enough with their shields around their shoulders, but I had carelessly left my cloak behind, not thinking I would get so cold, and had gone out with nothing but my shirt and shield. When the night was two-thirds gone and the stars had shifted position, I nudged Odysseus, who was lying close beside me, with my elbow, and at once he was listening.
“‘Odysseus,’ I said, ‘this cold will be the death of me—I have no cloak. Some god tricked me into setting out with nothing but my shirt, and I don’t know what to do.’
“Odysseus, who was as cunning as he was brave, came up with the following plan:
“‘Keep quiet,’ he said in a low voice, ‘or the others will hear you.’ Then he raised his head on his elbow.
“‘My friends,’ he said, ‘I have had a dream sent from heaven in my sleep. We are a long way from the ships—I wish someone would go down and tell Agamemnon to send us more men at once.’

“At this Thoas, son of Andraemon, threw off his cloak and ran off toward the ships, and I took the cloak and lay in it comfortably enough until morning. If only I were still young and strong as I was in those days, one of you swineherds would give me a cloak, both out of good will and out of respect for a brave soldier. But now people look down on me because my clothes are shabby.”

And Eumaeus answered, “Old man, you have told us an excellent story, and so far you have said nothing that is not quite satisfactory. For now, then, you will want for neither clothing nor anything else a stranger in trouble might reasonably expect. But tomorrow morning you’ll have to put your own old rags back on, for we don’t have many spare cloaks or shirts up here—every man has only the one. When Odysseus’s son comes home again, he will give you both a cloak and a shirt and send you wherever you wish to go.”

With that he got up and made a bed for Odysseus by throwing some goatskins and sheepskins on the ground in front of the fire. Odysseus lay down there, and Eumaeus covered him with a great heavy cloak he kept as a spare for extraordinarily bad weather.

So Odysseus slept, and the young men slept nearby. But the swineherd did not like sleeping away from his pigs, so he got ready to go out, and Odysseus was glad to see how he looked after his master’s property in his absence. First he slung his sword over his broad shoulders and put on a thick cloak against the wind. He also took the skin of a large, well-fed goat and a javelin, in case of attack by men or dogs. Thus equipped, he went to settle down where the pigs were bedded, under an overhanging rock that sheltered them from the north wind.
